intro: Eight notes, thirty variations, and an ending that stays in E minor: Brahms’s last symphonic finale is merciless. At its centre, a lone flute and a trombone chorale briefly slow the tread.

sections.label: Theme · Eight wind and brass chords
sections.mNote: A rising line with a chromatic A♯

sections.label: Var 1–11 · Plucked strings, then running notes
sections.mNote: The eight-bar pattern passes through strings and winds

sections.label: Var 12–13 · Flute solo, then E major
sections.mNote: The bars double in length; oboe and clarinet answer

sections.label: Var 14–15 · The trombone chorale
sections.mNote: Low brass sing in E major

sections.label: Var 16–24 · Opening chords over a changed bass
sections.mNote: A minor launches the return to three crotchet beats

sections.label: Var 25–30 · C major, then descending thirds
sections.mNote: A quiet detour precedes the last variations in E minor

sections.label: Coda · Faster, with cascading strings
sections.mNote: The eight-bar pattern breaks open at Più allegro

relations.label: The harmonic cycle returns
relations.basis: The passacaglia uses recurring eight-bar harmonic cycles. These neighbouring passages sit inside the opening variations, where the listening note near 140 s describes the retained cycle; the relation is harmonic, not a claim of an unchanged tune. CENS diagonal mean 0.918, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 18 s (cache/form/brahms-4-finale.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Eight chords without strings
cues.text: Winds and brass announce eight chords; the strings wait. The upper line climbs from E towards B, sharpening A to A♯ along the way. These eight bars will return thirty times, sometimes buried deep inside the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 4, IV, bars 1–8, Simrock first edition (1886). Theme and thirty variations described by Kelly Dean Hansen: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach’s bass, sharpened
cues.text: The pattern comes from the closing chorus of Bach’s cantata Nach dir, Herr, verlanget mich, BWV 150. Brahms adds a chromatic note. A♯ makes the climb towards B more urgent, and gives the finale a note it can worry at all the way to the coda.
cues.evidence: Bach source and added chromatic note: Jan Swafford, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-4. Hansen identifies A♯ as the fifth note of the theme: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.

cues.title: A flute in longer bars
cues.text: The bars double in length, from 3/4 to 3/2. A solo flute draws a hesitant melody out of the same eight-bar pattern, with little off-beat chords from strings and horns. The orchestra leaves it room to breathe.
cues.evidence: Variation 12, bars 97–104; the score retains the note-value speed while changing the metre. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trombones sing
cues.text: In E major, trombones sing a chorale with bassoons and horns. Violas and cellos answer with short rising arpeggios. The phrases leave rests between them, and their promised cadences keep arriving late.
cues.evidence: Variations 14–15, bars 113–128; trombone chorale and delayed plagal cadences. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Unripe cherries in the mountains
cues.text: From Mürzzuschlag in August 1885, Brahms sends Elisabeth von Herzogenberg the first movement: “Cherries never get ripe for eating in these parts, so don’t be afraid to say if you don’t like the taste.” He adds: “I’m not at all eager to write a bad No. 4.”
cues.evidence: Brahms to Elisabeth von Herzogenberg, August 1885, quoted by Jan Swafford in his Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-4

cues.title: The opening chords return
cues.text: The opening chords come back with force, and 3/2 contracts to 3/4. A minor now stands plainly at the beginning, with A in the bass. The strings answer the winds with a descending scale.
cues.evidence: Variation 16, bars 129–136; changed bass, restored 3/4 and descending string scale. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A detour through C
cues.text: The late variations make a quiet detour through C major. Winds move in thirds over plucked lower strings; violas and violins pass triplet arpeggios between them. A bass rising by semitones pulls the music back towards E minor.
cues.evidence: Variations 26–28, bars 209–232; C-major passage and chromatic bass leading back to E. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html. The section boundary covers the late variation group.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The pattern breaks open
cues.text: Più allegro: faster. The eight-bar pattern can no longer contain the music. Winds and brass drive upwards against cascading strings, then linger on the theme’s chromatic note, now spelt B♭. Timpani rolls and pauses hold it there.
cues.evidence: Coda, bars 253–260; the former A♯ is written B♭ and prolonged. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E minor to the end
cues.text: The last cadences hammer home E minor. Three-note upbeats repeatedly drive into the chord, and the timpani roll under the final blows. Brahms leaves the G♮ in place.
cues.evidence: Coda, bars 289–311; E-minor cadences and final timpani roll. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The chords leave gaps
transitions.from: Theme · Eight wind and brass chords
transitions.to: Var 1–11 · Plucked strings, then running notes
transitions.how: The harmony repeats, including the A♯ that presses towards B, but the orchestra separates its attacks. Horns and timpani sound on the first beat, plucked strings on the second. The third beat is empty. Trombones join the plucked answer for the first four bars.
transitions.evidence: Theme and variation 1, bars 1–16; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.

transitions.title: Twice the room for the flute
transitions.from: Var 1–11 · Plucked strings, then running notes
transitions.to: Var 12–13 · Flute solo, then E major
transitions.how: A late dominant chord on B prepares the return to E minor. The metre changes from 3/4 to 3/2 while the note values keep their speed. A solo flute carries the melody through the longer bars, accompanied by short off-beat chords in horns and strings.

transitions.title: The oboe leads into low brass
transitions.from: Var 12–13 · Flute solo, then E major
transitions.how: A descending oboe phrase carries across the join, delaying the cadence from A major to E major. Trombones, bassoons and horns take over in chorale phrases. Violas and cellos answer with upward arpeggios; a horn line later links the two chorale variations.

transitions.title: A minor cuts across the chorale
transitions.to: Var 16–24 · Opening chords over a changed bass
transitions.how: The flute’s descending link breaks off on A minor. After the pause, winds restore the opening chords with A in the bass, and the broad 3/2 bars contract to 3/4. Strings enter with a forceful descending scale. The expected E-major cadence has slipped away.

transitions.title: The eight bars overflow
transitions.from: Var 25–30 · C major, then descending thirds
transitions.how: Wide string and horn leaps extend the final variation beyond eight bars. Timpani grow more insistent; an augmented chord hangs between E and C major. At Più allegro, winds and brass begin the rising theme over cascading strings, but its fifth note, respelt B♭, holds up the expected continuation.
transitions.evidence: Extension and coda, bars 249–260; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 4, Op. 98, full score (Berlin: N. Simrock, 1886, plate 8686; first edition)
source.locator: IV. Allegro energico e passionato, printed pp. 77–113; eight-bar theme, thirty variations and Più allegro coda.

timeline.note: Winds and brass announce the eight chords; trumpet and timpani emphasise the fifth, with A♯.
Horns and timpani mark the first beat, plucked strings the second; trombones join the strings for four bars.
Soft winds, horns and timpani over low strings, swelling to a marked forte.
Winds and brass join plucked upper strings; cellos and basses bow their arpeggios.
First violins sing above off-beat inner strings; bassoons join the theme in the bass.
Quicker wind and string figures; horns and trumpets hold chords.
Held horn and trumpet notes beneath soft strings and winds.
Solo flute unfolds the melody in 3/2 above off-beat violin, viola and horn chords.
Oboe and clarinet continue the slow variations, piano dolce.
E major: an oboe link, then trombones, bassoons and horns in chorale phrases.
The chorale widens: winds, horns, trumpets and trombones in soft chords.
Forceful return: winds and brass restore the opening chords; strings add a descending scale.
Full orchestra with timpani; the variations drive on in fortissimo.
Brief withdrawal: held wind and brass notes under pianissimo violin scales.
Tutti returns, fortissimo through the next variations.
Quiet wind thirds and plucked low strings give way to flowing string arpeggios.
Poco ritardando and crescendo: trombones and timpani return.
Coda, Più allegro: winds and brass drive the theme over cascading string arpeggios.

composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853, a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music. Robert Schumann heard a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen — New Paths. Publishers became interested. Brahms now had to live up to a public prophecy before most of the public had heard a note. The young man’s piano sonatas were enormous; the symphonies Schumann expected would take much longer.

Brahms’s father Johann Jakob earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. Born in Hamburg in 1833, he studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
